Let's kick things off with Chapter One: Building a Foundation for Political Engagement.
Now, if you’ve ever looked at politics and felt a little overwhelmed—or maybe even a bit cynical—you’re definitely not alone. For many young Africans and Nigerians, the world of politics might seem like a private club, guarded by old traditions and wary of fresh ideas. But here’s the thing: getting started in politics isn’t about making some huge, dramatic move. It all begins with a shift in how you see things—a choice to view politics as a space where you can grow, have real influence, and actually serve your community.
At the center of meaningful political participation is a positive, resilient attitude. I’m not talking about just hoping for the best or ignoring the tough stuff. It’s about genuinely believing that change is possible—even when it feels like the odds are stacked against you. The very first step? Realizing that politics isn’t some exclusive club. It’s open to anyone who's willing to learn, adapt, and stick with it.
Think about it like learning a challenging game. The rules might seem complicated, the players experienced, and yes, there will be setbacks. But if you approach it with patience and a bit of curiosity, the whole thing becomes a lot less intimidating. Instead of feeling helpless, try to see yourself as someone who can actually make a difference.
And let’s be honest, setbacks are pretty common—especially in countries where political systems are still growing and changing. You’ll run into things like bureaucratic slowdowns, powerful interests, and a public that might not always be quick to trust new voices. But the people who really make progress aren’t always the most talented. More often, they’re the ones who refuse to let setbacks knock them out of the game. Every obstacle becomes a lesson, not a final defeat.
Another big part of this foundation is a willingness to keep learning. Political engagement isn’t a one-time event—it’s a journey. Staying up-to-date with current events, digging into the history of political movements, and watching how successful leaders operate can help you build a deeper understanding of the landscape. In this way, curiosity becomes a real source of power.
There’s also something else you can’t ignore: self-awareness. Before you step into the public spotlight, take a little time to ask yourself—why am I doing this? Are you truly driven to serve, or is it more about personal ambition? Getting clear on your purpose will help keep you motivated when things get tough, and it’ll build trust with the people around you.
So, how do you start building this mindset in your everyday life? Here are a few simple steps:
Set aside a bit of time each day to read up on what’s happening in politics—both in your own country and around the world.
Try having conversations with people whose opinions are different from yours. It’s a great way to broaden your perspective.
And take a moment now and then to reflect on your own values—and think about how they match up with your political goals.
By starting small, the whole journey into political engagement feels a lot less overwhelming. Instead of worrying about changing the entire system overnight, you can focus on your own growth—and that’s what lays the groundwork for making a real impact down the line.
